claims.text: Certain high-performance titanium alloy components have microstructural sensitivities that make conventional fusion-welding repair ineffective because of hot cracking.
DED combined with in-situ cooling, tailored alloying, and real-time feedback will produce a metallurgically fused repair patch.
The enhanced DED process will refine the repair microstructure.
The enhanced DED process will minimize thermal gradients.
The enhanced DED process will eliminate or significantly reduce hot cracking relative to traditional fusion-welding repair.
The repair should be processed in an inert atmosphere with 500–1000 W laser power.
Cryogenic or liquid-nitrogen-cooled gas jets can keep the substrate well below its melting point during deposition.
The feedstock alloy composition should be precisely matched to the base material.
Real-time thermographic feedback can adapt laser power and scan speed during deposition.
The repaired interface will have a refined gradient microstructure and a narrow heat-affected zone.
Controlled laser energy, tailored alloy composition, and active cooling minimize the duration and spatial extent of local melting.
Real-time temperature feedback prevents extended liquid-phase formation in vulnerable substrate regions.
Improved thermal and compositional matching reduces thermal stress and cracking risk at a laser-deposited interface.
The proposed controls will facilitate strong metallurgical bonding.
The repair will have negligible hot cracking and a seamless metallurgical bond.
The repaired region's cyclic-load and high-temperature mechanical properties will be superior to or on par with conventional fusion-weld repairs.
Traditional fusion-welding repairs create extended heat-affected zones and are prone to hot cracking under aggressive operating conditions.
The enhanced DED repair will remain effective under high temperatures and cyclic mechanical loads.
Repair success depends on precise temperature control and accurate feedstock matching.
Prior literature supports controlled DED-type processing as a means of reducing hot cracking.
